chunks: "Skin effect is the tendency of AC current to flow near the surface of a conductor instead of uniformly through its cross-section, and it gets stronger with frequency.
The cause is the conductor's own magnetic field. The alternating current creates a changing magnetic field inside the wire, and by Faraday's law that induces eddy currents.
Those eddy currents oppose the main current in the middle of the wire and add to it near the surface.
Another way to see it: a current path through the center links more flux, so it has more inductance, and at high frequency the current prefers the lower-impedance outer paths.
The current density decays exponentially going into the conductor, with a characteristic skin depth delta equals square root of over ( pi f micro) . For copper that's about 8.
4 mm at 60 hertz, 65 µm at 1 megahertz and only about 2 µm at 1 gigahertz.
Once delta is smaller than the conductor, only that thin outer layer carries current, so the effective area shrinks and resistance rises roughly with the square root of frequency.

Practically, it's why switching-converter inductors and transformers have higher AC resistance than DC resistance, why people use litz wire or copper foil, and why high-speed PCB traces get lossier with frequency and care about copper roughness."
